intro: C2 es la maestría: estructuras que solo usan los hablantes cultos, modismos que no se traducen, participios que condensan ideas, concesivas y hipotéticas de matiz, cohesión de texto y la precisión de quien elige cada palabra. Diez lecciones y un examen con el temario de los exámenes oficiales de nivel C2.
goals: Usar el subjuntivo y las estructuras formales (I suggest that he be…, lest, whether… or not).
Entender y emplear modismos y lenguaje figurado frecuentes.
Condensar ideas con participios y oraciones reducidas (Having finished…, Seen from above…).
Elegir con precisión: matices entre sinónimos y lenguaje académico.
Conceder con much as, however hard y no matter.
Hablar de lo hipotético con it's time, would sooner, as if y as though.
Dar cohesión a un texto con referencia y sustitución formal.
Usar binomios, colocaciones avanzadas y énfasis formal (the very, whatsoever).

lessons.title: El subjuntivo y las estructuras formales
lessons.summary: I suggest that he be informed: el verbo en forma base tras ciertos verbos y adjetivos.

sections.heading: El subjuntivo tras suggest, demand, insist
body: Tras verbos como suggest, recommend, demand, insist, request, propose y tras adjetivos como essential, vital, important, se usa that + sujeto + verbo en forma base (sin -s ni to): I suggest that he see a doctor. It is essential that every member be present. La negación es not + verbo: that she not be disturbed.
En inglés británico se oye también should: I suggest that he should see a doctor.

examples.es: El médico recomendó que descansara una semana.

examples.es: Es vital que el informe se termine hoy.

sections.heading: Fórmulas fijas y were
body: Expresiones hechas con subjuntivo: so be it (que así sea), God save the King, be that as it may (sea como sea), far be it from me (lejos de mí), come what may (pase lo que pase). Were en hipótesis formales: if I were, were he to accept (si aceptara), as it were (por así decirlo).

examples.es: Sea como sea, debemos continuar.

examples.en: Were he to resign, the company would struggle.
examples.es: Si él dimitiera, la empresa sufriría.

examples.es: Pase lo que pase, estaré allí.

examples.en: Far be it from me to criticise, but the plan has serious flaws.
examples.es: Lejos de mí criticar, pero el plan tiene fallas graves.

examples.en: He is, as it were, the brains behind the whole operation.
examples.es: Él es, por así decirlo, el cerebro de toda la operación.

sections.heading: Lest, whether… or not, so as to
body: Lest = por si, para que no (formal, con subjuntivo): He left early lest he miss the train. Whether or not expresa indiferencia ante la condición: Whether or not you agree, the decision is final. So as to / in order to expresan finalidad formal; so as not to, la negativa.

examples.en: Write it down lest you forget.
examples.es: Anótalo, no sea que lo olvides.

examples.en: Whether you like it or not, it's the law.
examples.es: Te guste o no, es la ley.

examples.en: She spoke softly so as not to wake the baby.
examples.es: Habló bajo para no despertar al bebé.

examples.en: They spoke in whispers lest anyone overhear them.
examples.es: Hablaban en susurros para que nadie los oyera.

sections.tip: El subjuntivo no cambia con la persona: that he go, that she be, that it remain.

sections.heading: La inversión condicional: should, were, had
body: En el registro formal (cartas, contratos, avisos oficiales, discursos) se suprime if y se invierte el orden sujeto-auxiliar. Should + sujeto + verbo plantea una posibilidad poco probable o cortés: Should you need help… (si necesitara ayuda). Were + sujeto + to + verbo, una hipótesis sobre el presente o el futuro: Were the bank to collapse… Had + sujeto + participio, una condición irreal en el pasado: Had I known… (de haberlo sabido).

Con were también se invierte la fórmula if it were not for (si no fuera por): Were it not for… Y en pasado: Had it not been for… (de no haber sido por). En la versión negativa invertida no se contrae nunca el not: Had it not been, jamás «Hadn't it been».

examples.en: Should you require any assistance, do not hesitate to ask.
examples.es: Si necesitara ayuda, no dude en pedirla.

examples.en: Had I known about the strike, I would have taken the train.
examples.es: De haber sabido lo de la huelga, habría tomado el tren.

examples.en: Were it not for her support, the project would collapse.
examples.es: Si no fuera por su apoyo, el proyecto se vendría abajo.

examples.en: Had it not been for the rain, we would have won the final.
examples.es: De no haber sido por la lluvia, habríamos ganado la final.

examples.en: Were the government to raise taxes, consumer spending would fall.
examples.es: Si el gobierno subiera los impuestos, el consumo caería.

rows: If it had not been for…

sections.tip: Solo se invierten should, were y had. Con otros verbos no hay inversión condicional: «Did I know…» o «Came he…» con sentido de if son incorrectos.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes con el subjuntivo inglés
body: El español marca el subjuntivo con desinencias (que él venga, que ella sea), y eso lleva a pensar que en inglés hace falta algo parecido: una -s, un pasado o un to. Pero el subjuntivo inglés es simplemente la forma base, igual para todas las personas y sin cambio de tiempo: They insisted that he leave (no left), aunque la frase esté en pasado.

El segundo error es el calco de «sugerir a alguien que haga algo»: suggest, demand e insist no admiten objeto + to (I suggest you to go es incorrecto). Se dice I suggest (that) you go o I suggest going. Ojo, en cambio, con el doble sentido: insist y suggest también pueden afirmar un hecho, y entonces llevan el tiempo normal: She insisted that she had paid (aseguró que ya había pagado).

examples.es: Te sugiero que tomes un taxi; se está haciendo tarde.

sections.heading: Registro: británico, americano y fórmulas fosilizadas
body: En inglés americano el subjuntivo tras suggest, recommend o insist es lo normal incluso en la conversación. En inglés británico informal se oye a menudo should + infinitivo o incluso el indicativo (It's important that she knows), pero en un examen de nivel C2 y en la escritura formal el subjuntivo es la opción segura.

Quedan además fórmulas fosilizadas que conviene reconocer: if need be (si hace falta), suffice it to say (baste decir), heaven forbid (Dios no quiera), long live… (larga vida a…), be it… or… (ya sea… o…).

examples.es: La escuela recomienda que cada estudiante traiga una computadora portátil.

sections.tip: Should en estas frases no significa «debería»: es solo el sustituto británico del subjuntivo.

sections.heading: Modismos de conversación
body: Un modismo tiene un significado distinto del literal. Los más frecuentes aparecen en series, reuniones y charlas: break the ice (romper el hielo), hit the nail on the head (dar en el clavo), on the same page (de acuerdo), a piece of cake (pan comido), once in a blue moon (muy de vez en cuando), cost an arm and a leg (costar un ojo de la cara), under the weather (indispuesto, algo enfermo).

body: Think outside the box (pensar de forma creativa), cut corners (hacer las cosas a medias para ahorrar), go the extra mile (esforzarse más de lo exigido), in the long run (a la larga), learn the ropes (aprender cómo funciona algo), the last straw (la gota que colma el vaso), bite the bullet (afrontar lo inevitable).

sections.heading: Metáforas y lenguaje figurado habitual
body: Muchas palabras corrientes tienen un uso figurado: a flood of complaints (una avalancha de quejas), to weigh up the options (sopesar), a bright idea, a heated argument (una discusión acalorada), to shed light on (arrojar luz sobre), the heart of the matter (el meollo).

sections.heading: Registro: cuándo usar un modismo y cuándo no
body: La mayoría de los modismos son informales o neutros: funcionan en una conversación, un correo a un colega o un artículo de opinión, pero chirrían en un informe técnico o un ensayo académico. Allí se prefiere el equivalente literal: the argument does not hold water → the argument is unconvincing.

Además, algunos modismos que aparecen en todos los libros de texto suenan anticuados a un nativo: it's raining cats and dogs casi no se oye (se dice it's pouring o it's chucking it down en Gran Bretaña). En C2 se nota quién usa los modismos vivos y en su contexto, no quién sabe más.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes: el calco del modismo español
body: El error más delator es traducir palabra por palabra un modismo español: «tomar el pelo» no es take someone's hair, sino pull someone's leg; «meter la pata» no es put the leg, sino put one's foot in it. El nativo no entiende el calco o, peor, entiende otra cosa.

A veces los dos idiomas coinciden (romper el hielo = break the ice; dar en el clavo = hit the nail on the head), pero es casualidad. Antes de arriesgarte, comprueba que el modismo existe en inglés con esas mismas palabras, y fíjate también en la preposición: get the hang of it, no «on it».

sections.heading: Británico frente a americano, y modismos en la prensa
body: Varios modismos cambian de un lado del Atlántico al otro: touch wood (británico) y knock on wood (americano) para «tocar madera»; a storm in a teacup frente a a tempest in a teapot; a skeleton in the cupboard frente a in the closet; sweep something under the carpet frente a under the rug.

La prensa y los discursos juegan con los modismos y los dan por sabidos: the elephant in the room (el tema que todos evitan), open a can of worms (destapar un problema mayor), a double-edged sword (un arma de doble filo). Reconocerlos es clave en las preguntas de comprensión de C2.

lessons.summary: Having finished the report, she left: condensar dos ideas en una.

sections.heading: Oraciones de participio presente
body: Un participio en -ing puede sustituir una oración con el mismo sujeto: Feeling tired, I went to bed (= Because I felt tired…). Walking home, I saw an accident (= While I was walking home…). El sujeto de las dos partes debe ser el mismo.

examples.en: Knowing the area well, she offered to guide us.
examples.es: Como conocía bien la zona, se ofreció a guiarnos.

examples.en: Looking out of the window, I noticed the snow.
examples.es: Al mirar por la ventana, me fijé en la nieve.

examples.en: Not wanting to disturb him, I left quietly.
examples.es: Como no quería molestarlo, me fui en silencio.

sections.heading: Having + participio y los participios pasados
body: Having + participio pasado marca que una acción terminó antes que la otra: Having finished the report, she left. El participio pasado solo tiene sentido pasivo: Seen from above, the city looks tiny (= When it is seen…). Built in 1900, the bridge is still in use.

examples.es: Como había perdido las llaves, no pudo entrar.

examples.en: Exhausted by the climb, they rested.
examples.es: Agotados por la subida, descansaron.

examples.en: Having spent ten years abroad, he found it hard to settle back home.
examples.es: Tras haber pasado diez años en el extranjero, le costó volver a adaptarse a su país.

sections.heading: Reducir oraciones de relativo
body: La oración de relativo se acorta con un participio: The man who is talking to Ana → The man talking to Ana. The houses that were built in the 60s → The houses built in the 60s. También con infinitivo: the first person to arrive, the best place to eat.

examples.en: The people waiting outside are journalists.
examples.es: Las personas que esperan fuera son periodistas.

sections.heading: El participio colgante: el error que delata
body: En español es aceptable «Al llegar a casa, el perro me recibió»: el infinitivo puede tener un sujeto distinto del de la oración principal. En inglés no: el sujeto implícito del participio tiene que ser el sujeto de la oración principal. Arriving home, the dog greeted me dice literalmente que el perro llegó a casa. Es el dangling participle, y en un texto de C2 penaliza.

Hay una excepción: algunas expresiones fijas pueden «colgar» porque se refieren al hablante, no al sujeto: generally speaking, strictly speaking, judging by, considering, given (that), provided (that), assuming (that).

examples.en: Walking into the room, I noticed a strange smell.
examples.es: Al entrar en la sala, noté un olor extraño.

examples.en: Generally speaking, the reviews were positive.
examples.es: En términos generales, las críticas fueron positivas.

examples.es: A juzgar por su acento, debe de ser de Glasgow.

examples.en: Considering the circumstances, the team did remarkably well.
examples.es: Teniendo en cuenta las circunstancias, el equipo lo hizo notablemente bien.

sections.tip: Prueba rápida: pregunta «¿quién hace la acción del participio?». La respuesta tiene que ser el sujeto que viene justo después de la coma.

sections.heading: Participios con conjunción y construcciones absolutas
body: Muchas conjunciones admiten un participio en lugar de la oración completa: after/before/since/while/when + -ing (After leaving school, she travelled) y once/if/unless/until/when + participio pasado (Once opened, keep refrigerated; If asked, say nothing). Es el estilo de las instrucciones, las normas y la prensa.

La construcción absoluta lleva su propio sujeto y es claramente formal o literaria: The work done, they went home (terminado el trabajo). Weather permitting (si el tiempo lo permite) y all things considered (considerándolo todo) son fórmulas fijas. Con with se forma una variante muy frecuente: With prices rising, people are spending less.

examples.en: Once opened, the product should be kept in the fridge.
examples.es: Una vez abierto, el producto debe guardarse en el refrigerador.

examples.en: If asked, just say you don't know.
examples.es: Si te preguntan, di que no sabes.

examples.en: Weather permitting, the ceremony will be held outdoors.
examples.es: Si el tiempo lo permite, la ceremonia se celebrará al aire libre.

examples.en: The contract signed, the two sides shook hands.
examples.es: Firmado el contrato, las dos partes se dieron la mano.

examples.en: With interest rates rising, many families are cutting back.
examples.es: Con las tasas de interés subiendo, muchas familias están recortando gastos.

examples.en: All things considered, it was a successful year.
examples.es: Considerándolo todo, fue un año exitoso.

sections.tip: Después de once, if, unless y until, el participio pasado tiene sentido pasivo: Once opened = once it has been opened.

sections.heading: Registro y posición: dónde suena bien un participio
body: Los participios condensan, y por eso abundan en la escritura (narrativa, prensa, informes). En la conversación suenan rígidos: nadie dice «Having eaten, we left» en una cena con amigos, sino After we'd eaten, we left. Reserva los participios para escribir o para hablar en registro formal.

Algunos participios y adjetivos cambian de significado según vayan delante o detrás del sustantivo: concerned parents (padres preocupados) frente a the parents concerned (los padres afectados); an involved story (una historia enrevesada) frente a the people involved (las personas implicadas); the present situation (la situación actual) frente a the people present (los presentes).

lessons.title: Precisión y matices
lessons.summary: Big, large o huge; say, tell o state: elegir la palabra exacta.

sections.heading: Sinónimos que no son iguales
body: Big es neutro y cotidiano; large es más formal y para cantidades (a large amount); huge y enormous intensifican. Say introduce palabras (he said hello), tell lleva receptor (he told me), state es formal y afirmativo, claim sugiere duda (he claims to be an expert), mention es de paso.
Walk, stroll (pasear sin prisa), march (con decisión), wander (vagar), stride (a zancadas): el verbo preciso ahorra adverbios.

examples.en: The company reported a large loss.
examples.es: La empresa comunicó una gran pérdida.

examples.es: Él asegura que estaba en casa, pero nadie lo vio.

sections.heading: Intensificadores y gradación
body: No todo admite very: con adjetivos extremos (freezing, exhausted, furious, brilliant) se usa absolutely, utterly, completely; con los graduables (cold, tired, angry, good), very, extremely, rather, fairly. Rather suaviza; quite puede significar «bastante» o, con adjetivos extremos, «completamente» (quite impossible).

examples.es: Hacía un frío espantoso.

sections.heading: Lenguaje académico y preciso
body: Verbos: analyse, assess, demonstrate, indicate, imply, account for (explicar), attribute to. Nombres: evidence (incontable), findings, approach, framework. Conectores: hence, thus, thereby, whereby, notwithstanding (a pesar de, formal). Precisar: in terms of, with regard to, as opposed to.

examples.en: The data indicate a clear trend.
examples.es: Los datos indican una tendencia clara.

examples.en: This accounts for the difference in results.
examples.es: Esto explica la diferencia en los resultados.

examples.es: El método era defectuoso; de ahí que se repitiera el estudio.

examples.en: Quality, as opposed to quantity, is what matters.
examples.es: La calidad, no la cantidad, es lo que importa.

examples.en: The findings imply that further research is needed.
examples.es: Los resultados dan a entender que hace falta más investigación.

sections.heading: Falsos amigos de nivel avanzado
body: En C2 ya no fallan los falsos amigos evidentes (embarrassed, carpet), sino los que parecen inofensivos porque el contexto casi encaja. Eventually no es «eventualmente», sino «finalmente, con el tiempo»; actually no es «actualmente», sino «en realidad»; sensible significa «sensato», y «sensible» se dice sensitive.

Otros clásicos: assist (ayudar; «asistir a» es attend), realise (darse cuenta; «realizar» es carry out), deception (engaño; «decepción» es disappointment), compromise (concesión mutua; «compromiso» suele ser commitment), sympathetic (comprensivo; «simpático» es nice o friendly).

examples.en: Eventually, after months of talks, they reached an agreement.
examples.es: Finalmente, tras meses de conversaciones, llegaron a un acuerdo.

examples.en: It would be sensible to wait until the results are in.
examples.es: Sería sensato esperar a que estén los resultados.

examples.en: She's extremely sensitive to criticism.
examples.es: Es extremadamente sensible a las críticas.

examples.en: The survey was carried out in two phases.
examples.es: La encuesta se realizó en dos fases.

examples.en: Both sides had to make compromises.
examples.es: Ambas partes tuvieron que hacer concesiones.

sections.tip: Actually corrige o matiza lo anterior: I thought he was Irish; actually, he's Scottish. Para «actualmente», usa currently o at present.

sections.heading: Hedging: matizar con precisión académica
body: Un texto académico o periodístico serio rara vez afirma de forma tajante. Se matiza (hedging) con verbos como appear, seem, tend, suggest, indicate; con modales (may, might, could); con adverbios (arguably, presumably, apparently, relatively, somewhat) y con expresiones como to some extent, it could be argued that o there is some evidence that.

Lo contrario, reforzar (boosting), se hace con clearly, undoubtedly, it is evident that. El dominio de C2 consiste en elegir el grado exacto: cambiar proves por suggests no es inseguridad, es precisión.

examples.es: Estos resultados parecen respaldar la hipótesis.

examples.es: Podría decirse que es la mejor novela de la década.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes con la precisión léxica
body: Muchos errores persistentes nacen de que un verbo español cubre lo que en inglés son dos: decir = say y tell (He said me ✗ → He told me); explicar lleva el pronombre sin preposición en español (explícame), pero en inglés es explain something to someone (Explain me ✗). Discutir algo no lleva preposición: discuss the plan, no discuss about the plan.

Otros vienen de contar lo incontable: advice, information, evidence, research y furniture no tienen plural ni llevan a/an (an advice ✗ → some advice, a piece of advice). Y del verbo robar: steal se aplica a la cosa robada (They stole my phone) y rob a la persona o el lugar (I was robbed).

lessons.summary: Por mucho que, por más que, pase lo que pase.

sections.heading: Much as, try as, adjetivo + as
body: Much as I admire him, I disagree (por mucho que lo admire). Try as she might, she couldn't open it (por más que lo intentó). Adjetivo + as + sujeto + verbo: Tired as I was, I kept going (cansado como estaba). Son formas literarias o enfáticas de although.

body: However + adjetivo/adverbio + sujeto + verbo: However hard you try, you'll never beat him (por mucho que). Whatever, whoever, wherever, whenever: Whatever happens, stay calm. No matter + how/what/where: No matter what he says, don't believe him.

sections.heading: Even if, even though, albeit, notwithstanding
body: Even if (aunque, hipotético): Even if it rains, we'll go. Even though (aunque, real): Even though it rained, we went. Albeit (si bien, formal, + adjetivo o frase sin verbo): a good result, albeit a late one. Notwithstanding (a pesar de, muy formal) puede ir antes o después del sustantivo.

examples.en: Even if you apologise, she won't forgive you.
examples.es: Aunque te disculpes, no te perdonará.

examples.en: He accepted, albeit reluctantly.
examples.es: Aceptó, si bien a regañadientes.

examples.es: A pesar del costo, el plan siguió adelante.

examples.es: Aunque le habían advertido, siguió adelante con el plan.

sections.tip: Even if y even though no son intercambiables: even if plantea una hipótesis; even though, un hecho.

sections.heading: Contraste con las concesivas básicas: although, despite, nevertheless
body: Las estructuras de esta lección son variantes enfáticas o formales de las básicas, y conviene tener estas bien firmes. Although y even though van seguidas de una oración. Despite e in spite of van seguidas de un sustantivo o de -ing; si quieres una oración, necesitas despite the fact that.

Nevertheless, nonetheless, even so y all the same conectan dos oraciones separadas (aun así). Though al final de la frase es coloquial y equivale a «pero» o «de todos modos»: It was expensive. It was worth it, though.

examples.en: Despite having trained for months, she didn't finish the race.
examples.es: A pesar de haber entrenado durante meses, no terminó la carrera.

examples.en: In spite of the fact that it was raining, the match went ahead.
examples.es: A pesar de que llovía, el partido se jugó.

examples.es: El hotel era caro. Pero valió cada centavo.

examples.es: Las pruebas eran débiles; aun así, lo condenaron.

examples.en: I know it's risky. Even so, I want to try.
examples.es: Sé que es arriesgado. Aun así, quiero intentarlo.

rows: Although it was late, we stayed.
Despite the fact that it rained, we went.
It was hard. Nevertheless, we won.

sections.tip: Despite nunca lleva of: «despite of» es el error más frecuente. In spite of sí lo lleva.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes con las concesivas
body: El español usa una sola conjunción, «aunque», y el modo verbal marca el matiz: «aunque llueve» (hecho) frente a «aunque llueva» (hipótesis). El inglés cambia de conector: although / even though para los hechos, even if para las hipótesis. Traducir siempre «aunque» por although borra esa diferencia.

Otro calco frecuente es el doble conector: «Aunque estaba cansada, pero siguió» es incorrecto ya en español, y en inglés aún más: Although she was tired, she kept going (sin but). Y however en sentido concesivo necesita un adjetivo o adverbio: However hard I try, no «However I try» con el sentido de «por mucho que».

examples.en: Although she was exhausted, she kept working.
examples.es: Aunque estaba agotada, siguió trabajando.

examples.en: However much I practise, my accent hardly improves.
examples.es: Por mucho que practique, mi acento apenas mejora.

examples.en: No matter how carefully you plan, something always goes wrong.
examples.es: Por muy bien que lo planees, siempre sale algo mal.

rows: Although it's raining, I'm going out.
Even if it rains, I'll go out.
Even if it rained, I'd go out.
However hard I try… / No matter how hard I try…

sections.tip: «Aunque…, pero» no se traduce con los dos conectores: en inglés va although o but, nunca los dos.

sections.heading: Concesivas formales y literarias: for all, be it, admittedly, that said
body: For all + sustantivo equivale a «con todo su…, a pesar de todo su…»: For all his money, he was lonely. Be it… or… (sea… o…) es subjuntivo fosilizado: every citizen, be they rich or poor. Admittedly y granted reconocen un punto débil antes de rebatirlo.

That said y having said that matizan lo que se acaba de afirmar (dicho esto). While y whilst (británico, formal) al principio de la frase también pueden ser concesivos: While I understand your concerns, I cannot agree.

sections.heading: It's time y would rather / would sooner
body: It's (high / about) time + sujeto + pasado simple: It's time we left (ya es hora de que nos vayamos). Would rather / would sooner + sujeto + pasado simple para preferencias sobre otra persona: I'd sooner you didn't mention it. Sobre el pasado: I'd rather you hadn't told him.

sections.heading: As if y as though
body: Comparan con algo irreal: He talks as if he knew everything (pasado simple para el presente irreal). She looked as though she had seen a ghost (pasado perfecto para el pasado irreal). Si la comparación puede ser real, el tiempo es normal: It looks as if it's going to rain.

sections.heading: Suppose, what if, if only y wish con could
body: Suppose / supposing / what if + pasado: What if we told them the truth? (¿y si…?). Wish / if only + could: I wish I could fly. Wish + would para quejas. Otherwise y or else expresan la alternativa hipotética: Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late.

examples.es: Supón que ganaras la lotería: ¿qué harías?

examples.es: Si pudiera hablar con ella una vez más.

sections.heading: Wish e if only: presente, pasado y quejas
body: Wish + pasado simple expresa un deseo irreal sobre el presente (I wish I had more time: no lo tengo). Wish + pasado perfecto, un arrepentimiento sobre el pasado (I wish I had listened: no escuché). Wish + would expresa queja o impaciencia por la conducta de otro (I wish you would stop): no se usa con el propio sujeto (I wish I would ✗).

If only es igual pero más intenso o dramático: If only we had left earlier! Para un deseo sobre el futuro posible, el inglés no usa wish sino hope: «Ojalá apruebes» = I hope you pass. Es un error muy típico, porque «ojalá» cubre los dos casos en español.

examples.en: I wish I had more free time.
examples.es: Ojalá tuviera más tiempo libre.

examples.en: I wish I hadn't said that.
examples.es: Ojalá no hubiera dicho eso.

examples.en: If only we'd left ten minutes earlier!

rows: queja sobre la conducta de otro

sections.tip: «Ojalá» + futuro posible se traduce con hope, no con wish: «Ojalá te guste» = I hope you like it.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes: el pasado que no es pasado
body: Para un hispanohablante, un verbo en pasado habla del pasado. Pero en estas estructuras el pasado es irreal: habla del presente o del futuro. Por eso se oyen errores como It's time we go o I'd rather you don't come, en lugar de It's time we went e I'd rather you didn't come.

También se confunden would rather y prefer: I'd rather + verbo base (I'd rather walk, sin to), pero I'd prefer + to + verbo (I'd prefer to walk). Con otra persona: I'd rather you stayed, I'd prefer you to stay o I'd prefer it if you stayed. En if I were / was, were es la forma recomendada en registro formal y la única posible en If I were you.

examples.en: I'd prefer you to stay here tonight.
examples.es: Preferiría que te quedaras aquí esta noche.

examples.en: I'd prefer it if you didn't smoke in the car.
examples.es: Preferiría que no fumaras en el auto.

sections.tip: Si dudas, pregúntate: ¿es real o imaginario? Si es imaginario, el verbo retrocede un tiempo.

sections.heading: Condicionales mixtas y condiciones sin if
body: Las condicionales mixtas cruzan los tiempos. Condición pasada con resultado presente: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Tokyo now. Condición presente (un rasgo permanente) con resultado pasado: If she weren't so stubborn, she would have apologised.

Otras formas de plantear la condición: but for + sustantivo (de no ser por), otherwise (si no), assuming / supposing (suponiendo que), provided / providing / on condition that (siempre que, con la condición de que).

examples.en: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Tokyo now.
examples.es: Si hubiera aceptado ese trabajo, ahora estaría viviendo en Tokio.

examples.en: If she weren't so stubborn, she would have apologised by now.
examples.es: Si no fuera tan terca, ya se habría disculpado.

examples.en: Assuming the train is on time, we'll arrive at six.

examples.en: You can borrow the car on condition that you fill it up.
examples.es: Puedes llevarte el auto con la condición de que le llenes el tanque.

rows: I would be a doctor now.

sections.tip: But for equivale a if it hadn't been for / if it weren't for, y solo va seguido de un sustantivo.

lessons.title: Cohesión y referencia en el texto
lessons.summary: The former, the latter, respectively, hence, the above.

sections.heading: Referirse a lo ya dicho
body: The former / the latter (el primero / el último de dos mencionados), respectively (respectivamente), the above / the aforementioned (lo anterior, formal), this / that / these / those + sustantivo resumen (this approach, these findings), such (de tal tipo): Such behaviour is unacceptable.

examples.en: Tea and coffee are popular; the former in Britain, the latter in Italy.
examples.es: El té y el café son populares: el primero en Gran Bretaña, el segundo en Italia.

examples.en: Lucy and Tom are 12 and 15 respectively.
examples.es: Lucy y Tom tienen 12 y 15 años, respectivamente.

examples.en: All of the above applies to part-time staff.
examples.es: Todo lo anterior se aplica al personal a tiempo parcial.

examples.en: Such a decision cannot be taken lightly.
examples.es: Una decisión así no puede tomarse a la ligera.

examples.en: These findings challenge earlier assumptions.
examples.es: Estos hallazgos cuestionan supuestos anteriores.

sections.heading: Conectores de consecuencia y contraste formales
body: Hence / thus / thereby (de ahí, así, con ello), accordingly (en consecuencia), whereby (mediante el cual), conversely (a la inversa), by contrast, on the contrary (al contrario, para negar), in turn (a su vez), that is to say / namely (es decir).

examples.en: Sales fell; hence the decision to close two branches.
examples.es: Las ventas cayeron; de ahí la decisión de cerrar dos sucursales.

examples.en: The new system, whereby staff work from home, has been a success.
examples.es: El nuevo sistema, por el cual el personal trabaja desde casa, ha sido un éxito.

examples.en: It's not a failure; on the contrary, it's a first step.
examples.es: No es un fracaso; al contrario, es un primer paso.

examples.en: The rules have changed, and we have adjusted our policy accordingly.
examples.es: Las normas han cambiado y hemos ajustado nuestra política en consecuencia.

examples.en: Some students thrive on exams; conversely, others do better with coursework.
examples.es: Algunos estudiantes rinden mejor en los exámenes; a la inversa, a otros les va mejor con los trabajos.

sections.heading: Sustitución y elipsis en textos
body: Para no repetir: do so, the same, likewise, so (I think so), one(s), that/those of, el verbo omitido tras auxiliar (as they should). Likewise y similarly abren frases paralelas; the same goes for / applies to extiende una afirmación.

examples.en: The north voted against the plan; the south did likewise.
examples.es: El norte votó contra el plan; el sur hizo lo mismo.

examples.en: The same applies to foreign students.
examples.es: Lo mismo se aplica a los estudiantes extranjeros.

examples.en: Those who wish to object may do so in writing.
examples.es: Quienes deseen objetar pueden hacerlo por escrito.

examples.en: If you haven't paid yet, please do so by Friday.
examples.es: Si todavía no has pagado, hazlo antes del viernes.

sections.tip: On the contrary niega lo anterior; by contrast solo compara. No son intercambiables.

sections.heading: Therefore, thus, hence, thereby: diferencias finas
body: Los cuatro expresan consecuencia, pero no se construyen igual. Therefore es el neutro y va con una oración completa. Thus es más formal y, además de una oración, admite -ing con el sentido de «con lo cual»: The engine uses less fuel, thus reducing emissions.

Hence suele ir con un sintagma nominal, sin verbo: hence the delay, hence its name (de ahí el retraso, de ahí su nombre). Thereby va con -ing y significa «con ello, de ese modo»: They cut prices, thereby attracting new customers.

examples.en: The council closed the bridge, thereby forcing drivers to take a long detour.
examples.es: La municipalidad cerró el puente, con lo cual obligó a los conductores a dar un largo rodeo.

examples.en: The town was built on a hill; hence its name, Highbury.
examples.es: El pueblo se construyó sobre una colina; de ahí su nombre, Highbury.

examples.en: The new engine uses less fuel, thus reducing emissions.
examples.es: El nuevo motor consume menos combustible, con lo que reduce las emisiones.

examples.en: He was not present at the meeting and therefore cannot be blamed.
examples.es: No estuvo presente en la reunión y, por lo tanto, no se le puede culpar.

rows: It is late; therefore, we must hurry.

sections.tip: Hence the delay (sin verbo) es perfecto; si necesitas un verbo conjugado, usa therefore o as a result.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes en la cohesión
body: «Por otro lado» en español sirve tanto para contrastar como para añadir («es barato; por otro lado, está cerca»). On the other hand solo contrasta; para añadir se usa moreover, furthermore, what is more o besides. Además, la preposición es fija: on the other hand, nunca «in the other hand».

«Al final» tiene dos traducciones: in the end (finalmente, tras un proceso) y at the end of (al final de algo concreto: at the end of the film). Besides no lleva of (besides that), y the former / the latter solo sirven cuando se han mencionado exactamente dos elementos.

examples.en: The flat is small; on the other hand, it's very central.
examples.es: El departamento es pequeño; por otro lado, es muy céntrico.

examples.en: The flat is cheap. Moreover, it's close to the station.
examples.es: El departamento es barato. Además, está cerca de la estación.

examples.en: In the end, we decided to stay.
examples.es: Al final, decidimos quedarnos.

examples.en: At the end of the film, everyone was in tears.
examples.es: Al final de la película, todos lloraban.

examples.en: Unemployment rose sharply. This trend worried economists.
examples.es: El desempleo subió mucho. Esta tendencia preocupó a los economistas.

rows: on the other hand solo contrasta
the former / the latter solo con dos

sections.tip: Un this suelto al principio de la frase puede ser ambiguo: añade un sustantivo resumen (this trend, this decision) y el texto gana claridad.

sections.heading: Sustitución en la conversación: so, not y la elipsis
body: En la conversación, so y not sustituyen una oración entera tras think, hope, expect, suppose, be afraid: I think so, I hope not, I'm afraid so. Con think, expect y suppose la negativa natural es I don't think so; I think not existe, pero suena formal o tajante. Con hope y be afraid solo cabe not: I hope not, I'm afraid not.

La elipsis tras auxiliar evita repetir el verbo: She said she would call, and she did. I didn't enjoy it, and neither did my sister. Es una marca de inglés natural: repetir el verbo entero suena mecánico.

lessons.title: Binomios, colocaciones avanzadas y énfasis formal
lessons.summary: Safe and sound, by and large, the very idea, no reason whatsoever.

sections.heading: Binomios: pares fijos
body: Expresiones de dos palabras unidas por and u or, siempre en el mismo orden: safe and sound (sano y salvo), by and large (en general), sooner or later, more or less, give and take (ceder por ambas partes), odds and ends (cosas sueltas), pros and cons, wear and tear (desgaste), peace and quiet, now and then (de vez en cuando), sick and tired (harto).

examples.en: They arrived home safe and sound.
examples.es: Llegaron a casa sanos y salvos.

examples.en: By and large, the plan worked.
examples.es: En general, el plan funcionó.

examples.en: I'm sick and tired of waiting.
examples.es: Estoy harto de esperar.

examples.en: Every relationship needs some give and take.
examples.es: Toda relación necesita ceder por ambas partes.

examples.es: Tuvimos que aprender por ensayo y error.

examples.en: Let's weigh up the pros and cons before we decide.
examples.es: Sopesemos los pros y los contras antes de decidir.

sections.heading: Énfasis formal
body: The very + sustantivo (el mismísimo, precisamente): the very idea, at the very least. Whatsoever / at all tras un negativo: no reason whatsoever, nothing at all. In no way, by no means (de ninguna manera). Not in the least (en absoluto). Indeed refuerza: It was indeed a surprise. The + adjetivo en -est + ever: the best ever.

examples.en: The very thought of it makes me nervous.
examples.es: Solo pensarlo me pone nervioso.

examples.en: There is no evidence whatsoever.
examples.es: No hay ninguna prueba en absoluto.

examples.en: This is by no means the end.
examples.es: Esto no es, ni mucho menos, el final.

examples.en: I'm not in the least surprised.
examples.es: No me sorprende en absoluto.

examples.en: He had no intention whatsoever of apologising.
examples.es: No tenía la menor intención de disculparse.

sections.heading: Colocaciones avanzadas
body: Adverbio + adjetivo: bitterly disappointed, painfully shy, highly regarded, vastly overrated, blissfully unaware, perfectly reasonable. Verbo + sustantivo: strike a balance, pose a threat, draw a conclusion, foot the bill, meet a deadline, bear a resemblance to, run the risk of.

examples.en: We need to strike a balance between work and rest.
examples.es: Hay que encontrar el equilibrio entre trabajo y descanso.

examples.en: He was bitterly disappointed with the result.
examples.es: Quedó amargamente decepcionado con el resultado.

examples.en: They ran the risk of losing everything.
examples.es: Corrían el riesgo de perderlo todo.

examples.en: The new law poses a serious threat to privacy.
examples.es: La nueva ley supone una grave amenaza para la privacidad.

examples.en: Who is going to foot the bill for the repairs?
examples.es: ¿Quién va a correr con los gastos de las reparaciones?

sections.tip: Las colocaciones no se improvisan: «make a balance» no existe; se dice strike a balance.

sections.heading: Más binomios y trinomios: el orden no se toca
body: Los binomios son irreversibles: el orden está fijado por el uso, y a veces es el contrario del español. «Papel y lápiz» es pen and paper; «de un lado a otro», back and forth; «de carne y hueso», flesh and blood. Ups and downs (altibajos), first and foremost (ante todo) y odds and ends (cosas sueltas) completan la lista de los más frecuentes.

Los trinomios son aún más idiomáticos: ready, willing and able (dispuesto y preparado), lock, stock and barrel (con todo, por completo), hook, line and sinker (tragarse algo por completo), tall, dark and handsome. Se usan sobre todo en la conversación y en la prensa.

examples.en: He paced back and forth outside the office.
examples.es: Caminaba de un lado a otro frente a la oficina.

examples.en: All you need for this test is pen and paper.
examples.es: Para esta prueba solo necesitas papel y lápiz.

examples.en: They're my own flesh and blood.
examples.es: Son de mi propia sangre.

examples.es: El negocio familiar se vendió con todo incluido.

examples.en: She fell for his story hook, line and sinker.
examples.es: Se tragó su historia por completo.

examples.en: I'm ready, willing and able to start on Monday.
examples.es: Estoy listo y dispuesto para empezar el lunes.

sections.tip: Si inviertes un binomio, el nativo lo nota al instante: «sound and safe» o «cons and pros» suenan a error.

sections.heading: Énfasis con la estructura: oraciones escindidas e inversión
body: Las oraciones escindidas (cleft sentences) ponen el foco en un elemento: It was the noise that kept me awake (fue el ruido lo que…). What I need is time (lo que necesito es tiempo). All I want is… (lo único que quiero es…). Tras What… did / All… did va el infinitivo sin to: All I did was ask.

La inversión tras un adverbio negativo o restrictivo es el énfasis formal por excelencia: Never have I seen…, Little did they know…, Under no circumstances should you…, Not only is it…, but…, Hardly had we… when…, No sooner had we… than…

examples.en: It was the noise that kept me awake, not the heat.
examples.es: Fue el ruido lo que no me dejó dormir, no el calor.

examples.en: What really annoys me is his attitude.
examples.es: Lo que de verdad me molesta es su actitud.

examples.es: Nunca he visto semejante caos.

examples.en: Little did they know what was about to happen.
examples.es: Poco sabían lo que estaba a punto de pasar.

examples.en: Under no circumstances should you open this door.
examples.es: Bajo ningún concepto debes abrir esta puerta.

rows: It was Tom who broke it.
Never have I been so tired.
Not only is it cheap, but it's also fast.

sections.tip: Hardly va con when y no sooner con than: Hardly had I arrived when…, No sooner had I arrived than…

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes con el énfasis y las colocaciones
body: El español enfatiza con «mismo» o «mismísimo» («el mismo presidente lo admitió»), y el calco the same president dice otra cosa: «el mismo presidente (no otro)». En inglés el énfasis se hace con el pronombre reflexivo: The president himself admitted it.

Las colocaciones verbales son el otro gran foco de calcos: hacer una pregunta = ask a question; decir una mentira = tell a lie; cometer un error = make a mistake; dar un paso = take a step; lluvia fuerte = heavy rain. Ninguna se deduce: hay que aprenderlas como bloque.

examples.es: El mismísimo presidente admitió el error.

lessons.title: Verbos de percepción, causativos y make, let, have
lessons.summary: See him go, make him wait, let it be, get it done.

sections.heading: Verbos de percepción
body: See, hear, watch, notice, feel + objeto + verbo base (la acción completa): I saw her leave. + -ing (en curso, parcial): I saw her leaving. En pasiva, el verbo base pasa a to: She was seen to leave.

examples.en: I heard the door slam.

examples.es: ¿Notaste a alguien comportándose de forma sospechosa?

examples.en: I felt the ground shake beneath my feet.

sections.heading: Make, let, have, get
body: Make + objeto + verbo base (obligar): They made us wait. Let + objeto + verbo base (permitir): Let him go. Have + objeto + verbo base (encargar a alguien): I'll have my assistant call you. Get + objeto + to + verbo (convencer): I got him to help. En pasiva, make lleva to: We were made to wait.

examples.es: El profesor nos hizo reescribir el ensayo.

sections.heading: Have / get something done y get + -ing
body: Have / get + objeto + participio: que otro haga algo (We had the roof repaired) o algo que te ocurre (He had his car stolen). Get + -ing: ponerse a (Let's get going). Get + objeto + -ing: poner en marcha (She got the engine running).

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes con hacer y dejar
body: «Hacer + infinitivo» se reparte en inglés entre make (obligar o provocar: The film made me cry), have (encargar: I had the car serviced) y get (conseguir: I got him to help). El calco más común es añadir to a make en activa (He made me to wait ✗) o usar make para un servicio (I made my hair cut ✗ → I had my hair cut).

«Dejar» también se divide: let es permitir (Let me go) y leave es abandonar o no tocar (Leave me alone). Let nunca lleva to (Let me to explain ✗), mientras que allow y permit sí lo llevan: They allowed us to go.

sections.heading: Más causativos: cause, force, have someone doing
body: En registro formal, cause + objeto + to + verbo expresa una causa sin intención: The storm caused the river to burst its banks. Force, compel y oblige (obligar con más fuerza que make) y persuade, convince (convencer) también llevan to. Help admite las dos formas: help me (to) move.

Have + objeto + -ing significa «conseguir que alguien acabe haciendo algo»: I'll have you speaking English in six months. En negativa, won't have + objeto + -ing expresa que no se tolerará algo: I won't have you talking to me like that.

examples.en: The storm caused the river to burst its banks.
examples.es: La tormenta hizo que el río se desbordara.

examples.en: The scandal forced the minister to resign.
examples.es: El escándalo obligó al ministro a renunciar.

sections.heading: Get frente a have: registro y pasivas con get
body: Get something done es más coloquial que have something done y a veces sugiere esfuerzo: I must get this report finished by noon (terminarlo yo mismo, por fin). Get también forma una pasiva informal para hechos inesperados o negativos: get fired, get hurt, get stolen.
En inglés británico need + -ing tiene sentido pasivo: The windows need cleaning (= need to be cleaned). Es una forma natural de hablar de tareas pendientes sin decir quién las hará.

examples.en: I must get this report finished by noon.
examples.es: Tengo que terminar este informe antes del mediodía.

examples.en: He got fired for being late too often.
examples.es: Lo despidieron por llegar tarde demasiadas veces.

examples.en: You should get that cough looked at.

examples.en: The windows really need cleaning.
examples.es: Las ventanas necesitan una buena limpieza.

sections.tip: Get + participio suena coloquial; en un escrito formal prefiere have something done o la pasiva con be.

lessons.title: Puntuación y estilo en inglés
lessons.summary: Comas, punto y coma, guiones y las diferencias con el español.

sections.heading: La coma
body: Separa elementos de una lista (a veces con la coma de Oxford antes de and: red, white, and blue), oraciones subordinadas al inicio (If you're tired, rest), oraciones explicativas (My brother, who lives in Lima, …) y conectores (However, …). No se usa coma entre sujeto y verbo ni antes de that.

examples.en: After the meeting, we went for lunch.
examples.es: Después de la reunión, fuimos a almorzar.

examples.en: She said that she was tired.
examples.es: Dijo que estaba cansada (sin coma antes de that).

examples.en: We bought apples, pears and plums.
examples.es: Compramos manzanas, peras y ciruelas.

examples.en: My sister, who lives in Lima, is a doctor.
examples.es: Mi hermana, que vive en Lima, es médica.

examples.en: However, the results were disappointing.
examples.es: Sin embargo, los resultados fueron decepcionantes.

sections.heading: Punto y coma, dos puntos y guion largo
body: El punto y coma une dos oraciones completas relacionadas (The rain stopped; the sun came out) y separa elementos largos de una lista. Los dos puntos introducen una explicación o una lista (There's one problem: money). El guion largo (—) marca un inciso enfático en estilo informal o periodístico.

examples.en: I have two passions: music and cooking.
examples.es: Tengo dos pasiones: la música y la cocina.

examples.en: The results were clear; nobody argued.
examples.es: Los resultados fueron claros; nadie discutió.

examples.en: She finally arrived — two hours late.
examples.es: Por fin llegó, dos horas tarde.

examples.en: The panel included Ana Ruiz, a lawyer; Tom Hill, an architect; and Mei Chen, a nurse.
examples.es: El jurado estaba formado por Ana Ruiz, abogada; Tom Hill, arquitecto; y Mei Chen, enfermera.

sections.heading: Diferencias con el español
body: En inglés no hay signos de apertura (¿ ¡). Las mayúsculas van en días, meses, idiomas, nacionalidades y en I. Las comillas suelen ser dobles en inglés americano y la puntuación va dentro: "Come in," she said. Los números: 1,000 (miles con coma) y 3.5 (decimal con punto).

examples.en: "Where are you going?" he asked.
examples.es: «¿Adónde vas?», preguntó.

examples.en: The population is 2,500,000.
examples.es: La población es de 2.500.000.

examples.en: I speak Spanish and English.
examples.es: Hablo español e inglés (idiomas con mayúscula).

examples.en: Classes start on Monday, 3 September.
examples.es: Las clases empiezan el lunes 3 de septiembre.

sections.tip: Its sin apóstrofo es posesivo; it's es it is o it has. Es el error de puntuación más común entre nativos.

sections.heading: Relativas especificativas y explicativas: la coma cambia el sentido
body: Una relativa especificativa (defining) restringe el sustantivo y va sin comas: The students who passed received a certificate (solo los que aprobaron). Una explicativa (non-defining) añade información sobre algo ya identificado y va entre comas: The students, who passed, received a certificate (todos aprobaron).

En las explicativas no se puede usar that: Madrid, which is the capital…, nunca «Madrid, that is…». Y cuando which se refiere a toda la oración anterior (lo cual), también va tras coma: He lied, which upset everyone.

examples.en: The students who passed the exam received a certificate.
examples.es: Los estudiantes que aprobaron el examen recibieron un certificado (solo esos).

examples.en: The students, who passed the exam, received a certificate.
examples.es: Los estudiantes, que aprobaron el examen, recibieron un certificado (todos aprobaron).

examples.en: He failed his driving test again, which surprised nobody.
examples.es: Volvió a reprobar el examen de manejo, lo cual no sorprendió a nadie.

examples.en: Paris, which I visited last spring, is beautiful at that time of year.
examples.es: París, que visité la primavera pasada, es preciosa en esa época del año.

rows: The book that I lent you is rare.
This book, which I love, is rare.

sections.tip: Nunca uses that justo después de una coma en una relativa: tras la coma va which, who o whom.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes: la coma que une oraciones
body: En español informal es frecuente unir dos oraciones completas con una coma («Era tarde, nos fuimos»). En inglés es un error con nombre propio, el comma splice, y en un texto de C2 se penaliza. Se corrige con un punto, un punto y coma, una conjunción (and, but, so) o una subordinada.

El caso más frecuente es however entre dos oraciones: no basta con comas, porque however no es una conjunción sino un adverbio. Va con punto y coma antes y coma después: I agree; however, there is a problem. También es un calco poner coma entre el sujeto y el verbo cuando el sujeto es largo: The students who passed the exam, received… ✗.

examples.en: It was late; however, nobody wanted to leave.
examples.es: Era tarde; sin embargo, nadie quería irse.

examples.en: It was late, but nobody wanted to leave.
examples.es: Era tarde, pero nadie quería irse.

examples.en: The shop was closed, so we went home.
examples.es: La tienda estaba cerrada, así que nos fuimos a casa.

examples.en: Everyone who attended the course received a certificate.
examples.es: Todos los que asistieron al curso recibieron un certificado.

rows: It was late, we went home.
It was late, so we went home.
I agree, however, there is a problem.
I agree; however, there is a problem.
She's clever, but she never studies.

sections.tip: However entre dos oraciones completas pide punto y coma antes y coma después: …; however, …

sections.heading: Estilo: paralelismo, concisión y diferencias británico-americanas
body: El paralelismo exige que los elementos de una lista tengan la misma forma gramatical: She enjoys swimming, reading and cycling (no «swimming, to read and cycling»). La concisión elimina redundancias (past history → history, free gift → gift) y prefiere la voz activa cuando el agente importa: The committee rejected the proposal es más claro que The proposal was rejected by the committee.

El inglés británico y el americano difieren en ortografía (colour / color, centre / center, organise / organize) y en puntuación: el británico suele usar comillas simples y Mr o Dr sin punto; el americano, comillas dobles y Mr. o Dr. Al citar un fragmento, el británico deja el punto fuera de las comillas si no forma parte de la cita; el americano lo pone siempre dentro.

examples.es: Le gusta nadar, leer y andar en bicicleta.

lessons.title: Comprensión lectora y auditiva
lessons.summary: Literatura, prensa de calidad y debate: la lectura experta.

sections.heading: Textos literarios y de prensa
body: En C2 se leen fragmentos de novela, columnas de estilo elaborado y textos académicos. La dificultad está en la sintaxis (incisos, inversiones, elipsis) y en el léxico de registro alto o figurado. Lee por unidades de sentido, no palabra a palabra, y reconstruye quién hace qué a quién antes de interpretar.

examples.en: What she had not expected, having rehearsed every objection, was indifference.
examples.es: Lo que no esperaba, tras haber ensayado cada objeción, era la indiferencia.

examples.en: Rarely has a book so slim carried so much weight.
examples.es: Rara vez un libro tan delgado ha pesado tanto.

examples.en: The town, such as it was, consisted of a church and a petrol station.
examples.es: El pueblo, si así podía llamarse, consistía en una iglesia y una gasolinera.

examples.en: Only later did she understand what he had meant.
examples.es: Solo más tarde entendió lo que él había querido decir.

sections.heading: Implicatura y presuposición
body: Lo que un texto presupone (da por sabido) y lo que implica (deja deducir) son el núcleo de las preguntas de C2. «Incluso su editor se sorprendió» presupone que el editor es quien menos debería sorprenderse. «Volvió a fracasar» presupone fracasos anteriores. Lee los adverbios con lupa: even, again, still, only, merely.

examples.en: Even her publisher was surprised by the book's success.
examples.es: Hasta su editor se sorprendió del éxito del libro.

examples.en: He merely repeated what everyone already knew.
examples.es: Se limitó a repetir lo que todos sabían.

examples.en: She still believes the letter was genuine.
examples.es: Ella sigue creyendo que la carta era auténtica.

examples.en: He only just made it to the airport.
examples.es: Llegó al aeropuerto por un pelo.

sections.heading: Escuchar registro y estrategia
body: En debates y entrevistas de alto nivel, los hablantes esquivan, matizan y reencuadran: with respect, that's not quite the point; I'd put it differently; if I may. Identifica cuándo alguien responde de verdad y cuándo cambia de tema, y qué posición defiende aunque no la enuncie.

examples.en: With respect, that's not quite the question I was asked.
examples.es: Con todo respeto, esa no es exactamente la pregunta que me hicieron.

examples.en: I'd put it rather differently.
examples.es: Yo lo plantearía de otra manera.

examples.en: If I may, the figures tell a less flattering story.
examples.es: Si me permite, las cifras cuentan una historia menos halagüeña.

examples.en: That is a fair point, but it rather misses the bigger picture.
examples.es: Es un argumento válido, pero deja de lado el panorama general.

sections.heading: Tono y actitud del autor: ironía y distancia
body: Muchas preguntas de C2 piden la actitud del autor, que casi nunca se declara. Se deduce de señales: so-called y las comillas de distancia (the «improvements») marcan escepticismo; la litote o understatement (not exactly a triumph) critica con suavidad; la hipérbole y la comparación incongruente suelen ser irónicas.

Los verbos introductorios también toman partido: claim y allege indican que el autor no da algo por cierto; concede y admit, que alguien reconoce algo en su contra; insist sugiere que otros dudan. Lee el verbo, no solo lo que se dice.

examples.en: The so-called reforms have changed very little.
examples.es: Las llamadas reformas han cambiado muy poco.

examples.en: The minister insists, somewhat implausibly, that nothing went wrong.
examples.es: El ministro insiste, de forma poco creíble, en que nada salió mal.

examples.en: It was not, it must be said, his finest hour.
examples.es: No fue, hay que decirlo, su mejor momento.

examples.en: The 'improvements' made the service even slower.
examples.es: Las «mejoras» hicieron el servicio aún más lento.

examples.en: She conceded that the figures were disappointing.
examples.es: Admitió que las cifras eran decepcionantes.

rows: el autor no lo da por cierto

sections.tip: En las preguntas de actitud, la respuesta casi nunca está en una sola palabra: suma el tono de todo el párrafo.

sections.heading: Errores típicos de hispanohablantes al leer y escuchar
body: Los falsos amigos siguen tendiendo trampas incluso en C2: eventually (finalmente), actually (en realidad), sensible (sensato). Igual de peligrosos son los usos menos conocidos de palabras corrientes: would para hábitos del pasado (He would sit there for hours = solía), while concesivo (While I agree… = aunque), hardly y barely como negaciones (apenas).

En las preguntas de opción múltiple, desconfía de la opción que repite palabras exactas del texto: en C2 la respuesta correcta suele ser una paráfrasis, y los distractores reutilizan el vocabulario del texto con otro sentido. En la escucha, atiende a los giros que cambian la dirección: but, actually, to be fair, having said that.

examples.en: He would sit by the window for hours.
examples.es: Solía sentarse junto a la ventana durante horas.

examples.en: I could barely hear what she was saying.
examples.es: Apenas podía oír lo que decía.

examples.en: The offer was not unattractive.
examples.es: La oferta no carecía de atractivo.

examples.en: She turned down the promotion.

examples.en: While I understand your concerns, I can't agree.

sections.heading: El examen C2: partes y estrategia
body: En un examen de nivel C2 (como el C2 Proficiency de Cambridge), la lectura incluye opción múltiple sobre textos largos (detalle, actitud, inferencia), un texto con párrafos eliminados que hay que reponer (cohesión) y preguntas de emparejar con varios textos breves. La escucha incluye fragmentos breves, una entrevista o debate con opción múltiple y una tarea de emparejar opiniones de varios hablantes.

La destreza común es la paráfrasis: reconocer la misma idea dicha con otras palabras. Practica reformulando: results fell short of expectations = the results were worse than expected; few would dispute that = almost everyone agrees.

exercises.title: Novel extract
exercises.text: The house had been sold, and with it the particular silence of its afternoons, which Helen now realised she had mistaken for peace. The new owners, a couple from the city with plans involving glass, had asked whether she wanted anything from the garden. She had said no, and then, absurdly, had driven back the following week to dig up a rosemary bush that had never, in thirty years, thrived.

questions.prompt: What does Helen realise about the silence of the house?
options: She had mistaken it for peace

questions.prompt: What is implied about the new owners' plans?
options: They will keep the house as it is

questions.prompt: Why is Helen's return described as absurd?
options: She went back for a plant that had never done well

exercises.title: Editorial: the price of convenience
exercises.text: Nobody voted for the disappearance of the high street; it was decided one click at a time. We mourn the bookshop while ordering the book, and the paradox is not hypocrisy so much as the predictable result of a system in which the costs of convenience are borne by someone else, somewhere else, later. The question is not whether we can turn back, which we cannot, but whether we are prepared to pay, in money or in patience, for the things we claim to value.

questions.prompt: How, according to the editorial, was the fate of the high street decided?
How does the author characterise the paradox of mourning shops while shopping online?
options: As the predictable result of a system

questions.prompt: What question does the author say really matters?
options: Whether we are willing to pay for what we value

exercises.title: Academic abstract
exercises.text: This study examines whether bilingual speakers show measurable delays in word retrieval compared with monolinguals, and whether such delays, where present, are offset by advantages in cognitive control. Across three experiments, bilinguals were marginally slower on picture-naming tasks but outperformed monolinguals on tasks requiring the suppression of irrelevant information. We argue that the two effects are not independent, and that the retrieval cost may itself be the mechanism through which the control advantage arises.

questions.prompt: What did the experiments find about picture naming?
On which tasks did bilinguals do better?
options: Tasks requiring suppression of irrelevant information

questions.prompt: What is the authors' central argument?
options: The retrieval cost may cause the control advantage

exercises.title: Satirical column
exercises.text: The company's new wellbeing programme, launched with a video of executives doing yoga on a beach, offers employees a free meditation app, a monthly fruit basket and a reminder that they may, if they wish, take their legally mandated holiday. Nowhere in the glossy brochure is the word 'overtime', which, like the word 'rain' in a holiday advert, is presumably thought to spoil the mood.

questions.prompt: What is the author's attitude to the wellbeing programme?
What does the reference to 'legally mandated holiday' imply?
options: The company presents a legal obligation as a gift

questions.prompt: What is suggested by the comparison with the word 'rain'?
options: The company avoids mentioning what is inconvenient
The office is by the sea

exercises.title: Literary interview
exercises.text: You've said you distrust the word 'inspiration'. I do, because it suggests the book arrives, whereas in my experience it is dragged out, sentence by reluctant sentence. What people call inspiration is usually the moment the dragging stops hurting. Does that make writing joyless? Not at all. There is joy, but it's the joy of a long walk, not of a gift.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer distrust the word 'inspiration'?
What does she say people usually mean by inspiration?
How does she describe the joy of writing?

exercises.title: Parliamentary-style debate extract
exercises.text: My honourable colleague describes the reform as a betrayal of rural communities. With respect, that is not quite the point. The question before us is not whether rural areas deserve investment, which nobody disputes, but whether this particular scheme, which has already cost twice its budget, is the way to deliver it. If I may, the figures tell a less flattering story than his speech.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker respond to the word 'betrayal'?
options: He says it misses the point

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say nobody disputes?
What criticism does he make of the scheme?
options: It has cost twice its budget

exercises.title: Science programme
exercises.text: For decades, the accepted story was that the dinosaurs were wiped out by a single catastrophic impact. That story is still broadly true, but it has become more complicated. Volcanic activity in what is now India had been stressing ecosystems for hundreds of thousands of years before the asteroid struck. Whether the impact was the cause of extinction or merely the final blow to an already weakened world is, as one researcher put it, a question of emphasis rather than fact.

questions.prompt: What has happened to the accepted story?
options: It remains broadly true but more complicated
It has been replaced by a volcanic theory

questions.prompt: What was happening before the asteroid struck?
options: Volcanic activity had been stressing ecosystems

questions.prompt: How does the researcher quoted characterise the disagreement?

exercises.title: Radio essay on handwriting
exercises.text: I was taught that handwriting revealed character, which may explain why I spent my childhood trying to have a better one. The truth, I suspect, is humbler: handwriting reveals mainly who taught you. Still, there is something in a handwritten page that a screen will never give: the record of hesitation, of a word crossed out and chosen again. We read not only what was written but how hard it was to write.

questions.prompt: What was the speaker taught about handwriting?
What does the speaker now believe handwriting mainly reveals?
What does a handwritten page offer, according to the speaker?
options: A record of hesitation and effort

exercises.title: Book review: a composer's life
exercises.text: There is a particular kind of biography that mistakes thoroughness for insight, and Margaret Hale's life of the composer Edward Lane, at nearly eight hundred pages, comes perilously close to being one. Every letter, invoice and lunch appointment seems to have been dutifully recorded. And yet, buried beneath the inventory, is a genuinely original argument: that Lane's famous silence in the last decade of his life was not a creative crisis but a deliberate refusal to repeat himself. Hale makes this case with quiet conviction, though she might have made it in half the space. Readers with patience will be rewarded; others may wish to start at chapter twelve.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's main criticism of the biography?
options: It includes too much detail at the expense of insight

questions.prompt: What does Hale argue about Lane's last decade?
options: He chose not to repeat himself
He was suffering a creative crisis
He was secretly working on a new piece

questions.prompt: What does 'comes perilously close to being one' suggest?
options: The book entirely avoids this fault
The book nearly falls into this category
The book is the best example of this kind

questions.prompt: Why does the reviewer mention chapter twelve?
options: It is probably where the most valuable part of the book begins

exercises.title: Opinion: the myth of the 'digital native'
exercises.text: The phrase 'digital native' has always flattered the young and excused the old. It suggests that anyone born after a certain date absorbs technological fluency the way children absorb a first language, without effort or instruction. The evidence, such as it is, points elsewhere. Teenagers are adept at the handful of applications they use daily, but surprisingly helpless when asked to evaluate a source, protect their data or write a formal email. Fluency in consumption, in other words, is not fluency in understanding. If schools continue to assume otherwise, they will produce a generation that can do everything with a phone except question what it is told.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, who does the phrase 'digital native' benefit?
options: Young people, who are flattered, and older people, who are excused

questions.prompt: What does 'The evidence, such as it is' suggest?
options: The evidence is limited, but it contradicts the popular view
The evidence confirms the popular view

questions.prompt: Which skill does the writer say many teenagers lack?
options: Judging whether a source is reliable

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main warning?
options: Phones should be banned from schools
Young people use technology too little
Schools must teach critical understanding rather than assume it

exercises.title: Podcast: the translator
exercises.text: Today I'm talking to Lucía Ortega, who translates novels from Spanish into English. Lucía, is a translation ever finished? Honestly, no. It's abandoned. There comes a point where the publisher needs the text and you have to let it go, even though you know that on page two hundred there's a joke that didn't quite survive the crossing. Does that keep you awake at night? It used to. Now I think of it rather like raising a child: you do your best, and then it goes out into the world and makes its own friends. Some readers will love a sentence I hated, and that's humbling.

questions.prompt: What does Lucía mean when she says a translation is 'abandoned'?
options: She stops when the publisher needs it, not when it is perfect
She loses interest in it halfway through

questions.prompt: What does she say about the joke on page two hundred?
options: It did not work as well in English
It was her favourite part of the book

questions.prompt: How has her attitude changed over time?
options: She worries more than she used to
She has learned to accept imperfection

questions.prompt: Why does she find readers' reactions humbling?
options: They sometimes love what she considered weak
They often complain about her choices

exercises.title: Radio discussion: planting trees
exercises.text: The council plans to plant ten thousand trees across the city. Doctor Patel, is this good news? In principle, yes. Trees cool the streets, absorb rainwater and, frankly, make people happier. But planting is the easy part. What do you mean? I mean that a young tree needs watering for three summers, and the budget covers one. The last time this was tried, nearly half the saplings died within two years. So you'd rather they planted fewer? I'd rather they planted the number they can actually look after. A thousand healthy trees are worth more than ten thousand dead ones, though they make a less impressive headline.

questions.prompt: What is Doctor Patel's overall view of the plan?
options: She supports the idea but doubts how it will be carried out
She thinks it is the council's best idea in years

questions.prompt: What is the main problem she identifies?
options: There is not enough space for the trees
The budget does not cover enough years of care

questions.prompt: What happened the last time a similar scheme was tried?
options: Almost half the young trees died
It was cancelled before it started

questions.prompt: What does her final comment imply about the council?
options: It has no real interest in trees
It may care more about publicity than results
It has planted too few trees in the past

exam.title: Short story opening
exam.text: By the time the letter reached her, the man who had written it had been dead for eleven years, which made its single request, that she forgive him, less an appeal than an instruction. She read it twice at the kitchen table and once more standing up, as if the posture might change the meaning. It did not. Then she did what she had always done with things she could not answer: she put it in a drawer and made tea.

Because it is written in capitals
Because she had already forgiven him

exam.title: Philosophy lecture
exam.text: We tend to assume that to understand a decision we must find its reason, as if every choice were an argument in miniature. Yet much of what we do is better described as habit, inclination or drift. This is not a counsel of despair. Habits can be examined and, with effort, changed; drift can be noticed. But the picture of the self as a perpetual deliberator is, I'd put it bluntly, a flattering fiction, and one that makes us worse at the reasoning we actually do.

questions.prompt: What assumption does the lecturer question?
options: That every decision has a reason behind it

questions.prompt: How does he describe the self as a 'perpetual deliberator'?
What is his attitude to habits?
options: They can be examined and changed

exam.title: Memoir: the receipts
exam.text: My father kept every receipt he was ever given. When he died, we found them in shoeboxes, sorted by year, the earliest dating from a bicycle bought in 1958. My brother saw in this a symptom of the anxiety that had shadowed our father's life, the fear that one day someone would demand proof and he would be unable to provide it. I was less sure. Leafing through the boxes, I began to read them as a diary written by a man who distrusted diaries: here the hotel on the honeymoon he never spoke of, there the hospital car park, paid for every day for three weeks in 1983. He had not been keeping evidence, I decided. He had been keeping time.

questions.prompt: How did the narrator's brother interpret the receipts?
options: As a sign of their father's lifelong anxiety
As a record of family holidays

questions.prompt: What does the narrator suggest about the father's attitude to diaries?
options: He thought they were a waste of money
He distrusted them, yet the receipts served a similar purpose

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the hospital car park receipts?
options: The father worked at the hospital
Someone close to him was in hospital for a long period
He often had trouble finding a parking space

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence imply?
options: The receipts were a way of preserving his memories
The father was obsessed with punctuality
The receipts proved that he had always been honest

exam.title: Feature: the return of repair
exam.text: For most of the twentieth century, repairing things was not a hobby but a necessity, and the skills involved were handed down as unremarkably as recipes. That chain has largely been broken. Products are now designed to be replaced rather than mended, their cases glued rather than screwed, their spare parts available, if at all, at a price that makes a new purchase look sensible. Against this background, the spread of volunteer 'repair cafés', where residents bring broken toasters and lamps to be fixed for free, might be dismissed as nostalgia. It would be a mistake to do so. The organisers are less interested in saving individual appliances than in changing what people expect of the things they buy, and in that, the recent wave of 'right to repair' laws suggests, they are beginning to succeed.

questions.prompt: How were repair skills passed on in the past, according to the writer?
options: As naturally as everyday knowledge such as recipes

questions.prompt: Why does buying a new product often 'look sensible'?
options: Because spare parts are expensive or impossible to find
Because new products are of better quality
Because home repairs are now illegal

questions.prompt: What is the writer's view of dismissing repair cafés as nostalgia?
What does the final sentence suggest about the organisers?
options: Their main aim is to save residents money
They want to change expectations, and new laws suggest they are succeeding
They hope to open their own repair shops

exam.title: Interview with a mountain guide
exam.text: Elena, you've guided climbers in the Andes for twenty years. What's the most dangerous thing on a mountain? People assume it's the weather or the altitude, and those are serious, of course. But in my experience the real danger is the summit itself, or rather, the idea of it. How do you mean? Clients have paid a lot of money and trained for months, so when I say we're turning back two hundred metres from the top, they hear failure. Some argue; one or two have even tried to continue alone. Have you ever regretted turning back? Never. I've regretted a few of the times I didn't. The mountain will still be there next year. The question is whether we will.

questions.prompt: What does Elena consider the greatest danger?
options: Climbers' determination to reach the top

questions.prompt: Why do some clients react badly when she decides to turn back?
options: They have invested so much that they see it as failure
They are afraid of the descent

questions.prompt: What does Elena imply when she says she has regretted some of the times she 'didn't'?
options: She once failed to reach a summit
She wishes she had climbed more mountains
Carrying on when she should have turned back had bad consequences

questions.prompt: What is the point of her final remark?
options: Mountains change from year to year
Staying alive matters more than reaching the summit
Climbing will be cheaper next year

exam.title: Lecture extract: how memory works
exam.text: We like to think of memory as a kind of archive, in which events are stored and later retrieved, more or less intact. The research of the last fifty years suggests otherwise. Each time we recall an event, we rebuild it, and in rebuilding it we change it, borrowing details from later experiences, from photographs, even from other people's accounts. This is why two siblings can remember the same childhood holiday in incompatible ways, both with complete conviction. None of this means that memory is worthless. It means that confidence is a poor guide to accuracy, which is a lesson the courts have been remarkably slow to learn.

questions.prompt: What view of memory does the lecturer challenge?
options: That memory is a fixed record that can be retrieved intact
That children remember more than adults

questions.prompt: According to the lecturer, what happens when we recall an event?
options: We reconstruct it and alter it

questions.prompt: Why does the lecturer mention the two siblings?
options: To show that families often argue about holidays
To illustrate that sincere memories can contradict each other
To prove that one of them is lying

questions.prompt: What criticism of the courts is implied?
options: They rely too much on how confident witnesses seem
